newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Kohl sticks by plan to cut jobless rate.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kohl sticks by plan to cut jobless rate.

text.p: German chancellor Helmut Kohl at the weekend said unemployment, measuring nearly four million people and standing near a post-war high, can be halved by the year 2000 as economic growth is expected to pick up soon.
Kohl made his comments in an interview with the Hannoverschen Allgemeinen Zeitung and an advance copy of the article was made available.

Asked whether he would stick to an earlier announced goal to slice the jobless rate by the end of the decade, Kohl said: "Yes, this goal has been formulated by employers and the unions, and I see no reason to change it."

Shrugging off suggestions that it may be impossible to halve Germany's 10.4 percent unemployment rate, which is considered to be one of the nation's toughest problems, Kohl said hard work could turn the plan to reality.
"Why shouldn't such a thing (like creating new jobs in west Germany in the early 1980s) occur again if we all roll up our sleeves."

Kohl based some of his optimism on signs Germany's economic recovery will soon pick up speed. "The prospects are not bad, I expect we we can count on seeing the economy grow at 2.5 percent next year," Kohl said.
But he acknowledged an economic upturn was no longer enough to automatically reduce unemployment rates. "We have to generate a few more ideas," Kohl said.
Greater job market flexibility, including more part-time work and a greater willingess among young people to run their own firms, would be steps in the right direction, Kohl said.
Regional governments disagreed with Kohl however saying the goal was too ambitious.

The states of Bavaria and Saxony, joint members of the so-called commission for the future, at the weekend said that the government's impact on cutting the jobless rate was minimal and that it was unlikely the jobless rate could be halved, German daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
